title: Create an agent that helps you think through decisions
description: A system that interviews you for your own decision criteria and weights, then builds a matrix that pressure-tests your reasoning.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: A comparison matrix is only as good as the criteria and weights someone put into it. Ask a chatbot to just help you decide and it can hand back its own opinion dressed up as a spreadsheet. This system interviews you for your own criteria and their weight first, then builds the matrix from what you said mattered.

Feed it a real decision, your options, and what you know about each one. It scores every option against your criteria with the reasoning shown alongside each score. Forcing the weights to add up to 100 surfaces disagreements about what matters that you didn't know you had, and it stops itself from guessing at information you haven't given it.
Run it once as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) for a single decision, or save the prompt and rules as a skill you reuse the next time a big choice comes up.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your decision and options, your criteria and their weights, the information you're still missing, and how you want the comparison presented.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that helps me think through a real decision. Ask me questions, one at a time, about the decision and options, what criteria matter and their relative weight, what information I'm missing, and how I want the comparison presented. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming your criteria and weights out loud, before you see any scores, keeps the matrix built on your judgment instead of the model's.

items: How many of your criteria are distinct, versus one concern restated twice.
Where your notes on each option live.
Whether this is a one-time build or a template you'll reuse for future decisions.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. The only [connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) this build typically calls for is a notes app or doc holding your research, [Notion](#tooltip-notion) or Google Docs. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build your system and test it on a real decision in front of you. The prompt below is an example. Your scope document gives a version for your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Build a weighted comparison matrix for a real decision and pressure-test my reasoning.

Context: Decision: [e.g., which job offer]. Options: [2-4]. Criteria and weights: [e.g., compensation 30%, growth 25%, location 20%, team 25%, confirm these total 100]. What I know about each option: [notes].

Rules:
- Score each option per criterion, 1-5, with reasoning shown, not just a number.
- Call out missing information instead of guessing.
- Flag any option where the weighted total contradicts my gut, and ask me to explain the gap.
- Never tell me what to choose.
- Output as a table: Criterion, Weight, and each option's score, then Weighted Totals and Gaps to resolve.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: showing the reasoning behind each score instead of just the number is what makes a 3 versus a 4 defensible instead of arbitrary.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Reasoning shown for every score, missing information called out instead of guessed, gaps flagged instead of buried?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what's off and fold the correction into the rules instead of patching the output by hand.

items: Save the weighting template so your next big decision starts from it.
Add a future-self pass comparing the 1-year outcome against the 5-year one.
Run the same matrix through a second AI tool and compare where the two disagree.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric) instead of a feel check. Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each comparison matrix, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, decision, weighted-total winner, option chosen, and outcome once I know it. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the pass/fail checks keep you from grading a matrix on vibes, and the log shows whether the math and your final choice ever pull apart.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few decisions straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that fails again and again is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. Don't let the tool supply your own criteria or weights, or the score is just its opinion in a spreadsheet. Watch for false precision too. A 3.7 against a 3.4 on soft judgment isn't a real gap.
